title: Chapter XXXIX

teacherSummary.text: Lydia and Kitty meet their sisters at an inn, chattering about officers and announcing that Miss King has gone. Lydia buys an ugly bonnet and dreams of Brighton, where the regiment is going.

vocabulary.definition: A bag for holding implements or materials for work
vocabulary.context: As soon as all had ate, and the elder ones paid, the carriage was ordered; and after some contrivance, the whole party, with all their boxes, workbags, and parcels, and the unwelcome addition of Kitty’s and Lydia’s purchases, were seated in it.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “workbag”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To lessen in price or estimated value
vocabulary.context: To this, Mary very gravely replied, “Far be it from me, my dear sister, to depreciate such pleasures.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “depreciate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A light box of pasteboard or thin wood, usually cylindrical, for holding ruffs (the bands of the 17th century),…
vocabulary.context: “I am glad I bought my bonnet, if it is only for the fun of having another bandbox!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “bandbox”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To turn or tip (anything) over from an upright, or a proper, position so that it lies upon its side or bottom upwards
vocabulary.context: Brighton, and a whole campful of soldiers, to us, who have been overset already by one poor regiment of militia, and the monthly balls of Meryton.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overset”: vers (Latin vertere, "to turn"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To form and occupy a camp
vocabulary.context: “They are going to be encamped near Brighton; and I do so want papa to take us all there for the summer!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “encamp”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: (Literally, called equally one thing or the other
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth saw directly that her father had not the smallest intention of yielding; but his answers were at the same time so vague and equivocal, that her mother, though often disheartened, had never yet despaired of succeeding at last.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “equivocal”: voc (Latin vocare, "to call") + -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth saw directly that her father had not the smallest intention of yielding; but his answers were at the same time so vague and equivocal, that her mother, though often disheartened, had never yet despaired of succeeding at last.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “despair”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: They would doubtless be congenial with the generality of female minds.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “congenial”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + gen (Latin/Greek genus, "birth, kind") + -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: The act of adding two or more things together
vocabulary.context: With such kind of histories of their parties and good jokes, did Lydia, assisted by Kitty’s hints and additions, endeavour to amuse her companions all the way to Longbourn.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “addition”: ad- (Latin ad, "to, toward"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Then showing her purchases: “Look here, I have bought this bonnet.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “purchase”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Brighton was a fashionable seaside resort with military camps.

significance: The decision not to warn others has consequences.
discussionQuestions: Were Elizabeth and Jane right to keep Wickham's secret?
Where does foreshadowing appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

items.prompt: Where does the regiment plan to go?

In the line “As soon as all had ate, and the elder ones paid, the carriage was ordered; and after some contrivance, the whole party, with all their boxes, workbags, and parcels, and the unwelcome addition of Kitty’s and Lydia’s purchases, were seated in it.”, what does “workbags” most nearly mean?
options: A light box of pasteboard or thin wood, usually cylindrical, for holding ruffs (the bands of the 17th century),…
To turn or tip (anything) over from an upright, or a proper, position so that it lies upon its side or bottom upwards
A bag for holding implements or materials for work
To lessen in price or estimated value

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXXIX,” how does Austen show the Brighton plan? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXXIX, how does Austen develop the idea of the Brighton plan? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the foreshadowing in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXXIX develops the idea of the Brighton plan. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of foreshadowing and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXXIX (where it begins, turns and ends) and its foreshadowing shape the reader's understanding of the Brighton plan. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXXIX suggests about the Brighton plan. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses foreshadowing in Chapter XXXIX to complicate the reader's understanding of the Brighton plan. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXXIX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the Brighton plan responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXXIX alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the Brighton plan follows or bends those conventions, using the foreshadowing as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXXIX and its treatment of the Brighton plan. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's foreshadowing and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXXIX as evidence for a larger claim about the Brighton plan in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXXIX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the Brighton plan. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events

I do not think it is very pretty; but I thought I might as well buy it as not. I shall pull it to pieces as soon as I get home, and see if I can make it up any better.”

annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

annotationFocus.label: Plot

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Were Elizabeth and Jane right to keep Wickham's secret? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are workbags, depreciate, bandbox, overset, encamped. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “As soon as all had ate, and the elder ones paid, the carriage was ordered; and after some contrivance, the whole party, with all their boxes, workbags, and parcels, and the unwelcome addition of Kitty’s and Lydia’s purchases, were seated in it.” Webster's says: A bag for holding implements or materials for work. Now the word history: “workbag”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “depreciate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “bandbox”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Brighton was a fashionable seaside resort with military camps. Why does this chapter matter? The decision not to warn others has consequences. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for foreshadowing.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see foreshadowing, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the Brighton plan.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of foreshadowing. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “And we mean to treat you all,” added Lydia; “but you must lend us the money, for we have just spent ours at the shop out there.” Then showing her purchases: “Look here, I have bought this bonnet. I do not think it is very pretty; but I thought I might as well buy it as not. I shall pull it to pieces as soon as I get home, and see if I can make it up any better.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Foreshadowing, Characterization, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXXIX,” how does Austen show the Brighton plan? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the foreshadowing you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the Brighton plan, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how foreshadowing shapes the Brighton plan. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
